newsitem.title: USA: Reno names two managers for naturalization problems.
newsitem.headline: Reno names two managers for naturalization problems.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said Friday two senior management officials will work at the Immigration and Naturalisation Service to deal with its problem-plagued citizenship programme.

She said the officials, former U.S. Comptroller General Charles Bowsher and Robert Bratt, a 19-year Justice Department veteran, will "address the pressing need to improve the integrity of the nation's naturalisation system."

The appointments came a week after the release of a critical review that found only one of 23 INS offices had been in full compliance with procedures for checking citizenship applications. Members of Congress also have criticised the INS, saying it granted citizenship last year to thousands of unqualified aliens, including some with criminal records, because of poor background checks.

Reno and INS Commissioner Doris Meissner said Bratt, an administrator at the Justice Department's criminal division, would become executive director for naturalisation operations. Reno said Bowsher will serve as a special adviser to Meissner, helping develop a plan to correct the widespread problems in the programme and carry out the new procedures.
Bowsher served as comptroller general, the head of the congressional watchdog agency the General Accounting Office, from 1981 until 1996. He will work in a part-time, contract position.

The review by KPMG Peat Marwick LLP found that only the Boston office had been meeting all the INS requirements put in place in November. It said seven other offices had been in marginal compliance and the rest failed.

Reno last month said another private accounting and cconsulting firm, Coopers and Lybrand, had been selected under a $4.3 million contract to improve the naturalisation system. She said Bratt's first priority will be to ensure that current naturalisation processing follows required quality procedures.
She also said he would implement recommendations stemming from the ongoing review by INS and KPMG Peat Marwick of the more than one million aliens granted citizenship last year.
Republicans in Congress charge applicants were rushed through so they could vote for Democrats in last November's elections.
